A four-part video teaching on the last days from a preterist viewpoint, summarised and corrected where its historical details go beyond the sources.
Transcripts were read for this study; the summary is paraphrased.

Some of Jesus' sternest words, such as “Depart from me, I never knew you,” Gehenna, “weeping and gnashing of teeth,” and “one will be taken,” are usually read as descriptions of the afterlife or the second coming. But Jesus spoke them in the language of the prophets, to a generation he said would see judgement fall. This study traces those warnings back to Hosea, Jeremiah, Isaiah and Malachi, follows them forward to the siege and fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 as Josephus and Eusebius record it, and asks which ones belong to that historical judgement, which look beyond it, and which do both. It includes a summary of a four-part teaching series on the last days.

Reading a warning in its first-century setting does not deny the final judgement. Scripture still teaches that Christ will return bodily, that all the dead will be raised, and that God will judge the world in righteousness (John 5:28-29; Acts 17:31; Hebrews 9:27; Revelation 20:11-15). Christians differ on the nature of final punishment; that question is not settled by this study. What it argues is narrower: many warnings usually quoted about the afterlife were first aimed at the coming destruction of Jerusalem, and should be heard that way first.

Part 1: Why the last days matter, and how to hold them
Views of the end are not a test of salvation and should never divide friends.
Every system is a possibility; what history shows actually happened is the firmest ground.
Fear-driven prophecy teaching, such as 1970s rapture films, can do real harm; God has not given a spirit of fear (2 Timothy 1:7).
Revelation is written in signs (1:1) to churches facing the Roman war, with a date before AD 70 suggested by the standing temple (11:1-2).
“It must get worse” theology can make the church passive; Jesus prayed that his people stay in the world, not be taken out (John 17:15).
The kingdom is righteousness, peace and joy in the Spirit (Romans 14:17), not escape.
Part 2: The four views of Revelation
Historicism read Revelation as church history and made the papacy the Antichrist; it was the Reformers' main view.
Futurism was developed by the Jesuit Ribera (c. 1590) in reply, though early writers such as Irenaeus also expected a future Antichrist.
Idealism draws timeless lessons, from Origen and Augustine on; it is valuable as application.
Preterism, first set out systematically by Alcázar (1614), reads the Olivet Discourse and much of Revelation as fulfilled in AD 70.
A useful rule: one interpretation, what the text meant to its first readers, and many applications.
A letter written to a first-century church was written for us, but not to us.
Part 4: The last days of what?
Hebrews 1:2 says its readers were already living in the last days.
From Genesis 49:1 on, “the last days” concerns Israel's covenant story and its climax.
The New Testament writers speak of their own time as the last days and even the “last hour” (1 John 2:18).
“End of the world” in older translations is better “end of the age” (Matthew 24:3).
For about forty years the old and new covenants overlapped until the temple fell (Hebrews 8:13; 9:8).
Warnings in Hebrews 6 and 10 first addressed believers tempted back to temple sacrifice.
Christians who heeded Jesus' warning fled to Pella and escaped the siege.
Part 5: Matthew 24, verse by verse
The great tribulation was unique for the Jewish people because it removed the temple, the centre of their whole national life.
“This generation” means Jesus' contemporaries; reading it otherwise lets critics call him a false prophet.
The signs fit the first century: wars after the Roman peace, martyred apostles, the gospel to the known world (Colossians 1:23), false messiahs.
The abomination of desolation is explained in Luke as armies surrounding Jerusalem.
The instructions about roofs, Judea's hills, winter and the Sabbath fit first-century Judea.
“Coming on the clouds” is the prophets' language for God judging through armies (Isaiah 19:1).
The future is the kingdom growing like leaven until every enemy is subdued (Matthew 13:33; 1 Corinthians 15:24-28).

How does Hosea 8 help explain “I never knew you”?
Hosea shows a people crying “we know you!” while rejecting what is good, with an enemy at the door. Jesus confronts the same contradiction in his generation.

In Hosea 8 Israel insists, “My God, we, Israel, know you,” yet has broken the covenant and transgressed the law; an enemy swoops like an eagle over the house of the LORD. In Matthew 7, people say “Lord, Lord” and list their works, but did not do the Father's will. Both are religious profession without faithfulness, and both stand before a coming judgement. Hosea's was Assyria; Jesus' warning, read in its setting, points to the day of the LORD on Jerusalem.
Hosea 8:1: like an eagle against the house of the LORD.
Matthew 7:24-27: the house built on sand falls in the storm.
Luke 13:26-27: “we ate and drank in your presence … I do not know where you come from.”
Most commentators read Matthew 7:21-23 of the final judgement, while agreeing that the Hosea background and the principle of profession without obedience are relevant.
What does it mean that Jesus “never knew” them?
In Scripture, “to know” often means to acknowledge as one's own in covenant love. He never owned them as his, whatever they claimed.

God said of Israel, “You only have I known of all the families of the earth” (Amos 3:2): chosen and owned. Paul says “the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19). To be “never known” is to have had a name for religion without belonging. That is why the cure is not more religious activity but doing the Father's will.
Amos 3:2: you only have I known.
2 Timothy 2:19: the Lord knows those who are his.
John 10:14: I know my own and my own know me.
This meaning holds whichever judgement is in view.
Where does “mountains, fall on us” come from?
From Hosea 10:8, describing Israel under invasion. Jesus applied it to Jerusalem on the way to the cross, and Revelation 6:16 repeats it at the great day of wrath.

Hosea said that when the high places of Israel were destroyed, people would say to the mountains, “Cover us,” and to the hills, “Fall on us.” Jesus told the weeping women to weep for themselves, for days were coming when people would say the same. Revelation's sixth seal uses the same cry. The line runs from Israel's fall, to Jerusalem's, in that generation.

What is Gehenna?
The Valley of Hinnom, beside Jerusalem: once a place of child sacrifice, then named by Jeremiah the Valley of Slaughter for Jerusalem's judgement.

The Greek word Gehenna comes from the Hebrew ge-hinnom, the Valley of Hinnom on the south and west of Jerusalem. Kings sacrificed children there (2 Kings 23:10). Jeremiah declared it would be called the Valley of Slaughter, filled with Jerusalem's unburied dead (7:32; 19:6). When Jesus warned Jerusalem's leaders of the judgement of Gehenna and said it would come on that generation, his hearers would have pictured that valley. The Hinnom map on this page traces its history.
Jeremiah 19:6: no more Topheth, but the Valley of Slaughter.
Matthew 23:33-36: the judgement of Gehenna … on this generation.
Gehenna appears twelve times in the New Testament.
By Jesus' day Jewish writings also used Gehenna for a place of punishment after death, and many read Jesus that way, especially Matthew 10:28.
What does Josephus record about the dead in the siege?
That the famine dead became too many to bury, were thrown from the walls into the valleys, and that Titus, seeing the valleys full, groaned and called God to witness that it was not his doing.

In Jewish War Book 5 (12.3-4), Josephus says the rebels at first buried the dead at public expense, but as the famine grew they threw them from the walls into the valleys. When Titus saw the valleys full of corpses and the decay, he groaned and, raising his hands, called God to witness that this was not his work. Later he reports deserters saying hundreds of thousands of bodies had been carried out of the gates (5.13.7), and he reckons 1,100,000 died in the siege (6.9.3).
Jewish War 5.12.3-4: the valleys full of the dead.
Jewish War 6.9.3: 1,100,000 dead.
Jeremiah 7:33: the dead bodies of this people will be food for the birds.
Historians treat Josephus' large numbers with caution, though the scale of the catastrophe is not in doubt.
What does “their worm does not die” mean in Mark 9?
Jesus is quoting Isaiah 66:24, where the faithful go out and look on the dead bodies of the rebels outside Jerusalem.

Isaiah's final verse pictures corpses, not living souls, consumed by worm and fire that do not stop until the work is done. “Unquenchable fire” in Jeremiah is the fire God would kindle on Jerusalem (7:20; 17:27). Jesus' hearers would have heard a warning of shameful death and disgrace in judgement. Whether and how it also describes final punishment is debated among Christians.
Isaiah 66:24: they shall go out and look on the dead bodies.
Jeremiah 17:27: I will kindle a fire in its gates, and it shall not be quenched.
Traditional readers see a description of unending punishment; conditional-immortality readers see final destruction.
Why does it matter that John the Baptist was Elijah?
Because Malachi said Elijah would come before the great and awesome day of the LORD. If Elijah had come, the great day was near.

Malachi ends the Old Testament promising Elijah before the day that burns like an oven. Jesus said, “If you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come,” and after the transfiguration, “Elijah has already come.” John preached the wrath about to come, the axe at the root, and the chaff to be burned. The great day followed within that generation.

Matthew 3:7-12: the wrath about to come.
Some futurists expect a further Elijah figure before the second coming (Revelation 11:3-6).
What was “the day of the LORD” in the prophets?
A day when God judged a nation in history: Babylon, Egypt, Edom, Samaria, Jerusalem. It came with cosmic imagery, but in real history.

Isaiah's day of the LORD on Babylon darkened the stars (13:10); Ezekiel's day on Egypt was a day of clouds (30:3); Zephaniah's day on Jerusalem was a day of wrath (1:15). Each came in history. Malachi and Joel promised a great day after Elijah and the Spirit; Peter said the Spirit had come (Acts 2:16-21), and Jesus said the days of vengeance were near (Luke 21:22). The timeline on this page lines up these days.
Isaiah 13:6-10 (Babylon).
Ezekiel 30:3 (Egypt).
Acts 2:20: before the great and magnificent day.
Futurists see these as patterns of a final day of the LORD still to come, which Paul and Peter also mention (1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Peter 3:10).
What was the flight to Pella?
Eusebius reports that Jerusalem's Christians were warned before the war and moved to Pella, east of the Jordan, escaping the siege, as Jesus had told them to flee.

Jesus said, “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies … let those in Judea flee to the mountains.” In AD 66 Cestius Gallus surrounded the city and then withdrew, giving an opening. Eusebius (Church History 3.5.3) says the church, warned by revelation, left for Pella in Perea. Epiphanius repeats the story. Some historians doubt it, but it fits Jesus' instructions closely.
Matthew 24:15-18: do not go back for your cloak.
Eusebius, Church History 3.5.3.
Futurists apply the instructions to a future flight from Jerusalem.
How can I tell whether a warning is about AD 70 or the final judgement?
Look for the audience, the time words, the place, and the Old Testament source. Then check whether the New Testament places it elsewhere.

Ask five questions. Who is addressed: Jerusalem's leaders, the disciples, or all the dead? Are there time words, such as “this generation” or “soon”? Is there a place, such as Judea, the temple or Jerusalem? Which prophet is quoted, and what was he warning about? Does another text place the event at the resurrection of all the dead? The flowchart on this page walks through these questions.
Matthew 23:36: this generation (AD 70).
John 5:28-29: all who are in the tombs (final).
Matthew 25:31-32: all the nations gathered (debated).
Futurists add that a near fulfilment can foreshadow a far one.
Why does reading these warnings historically matter?
Because it lets them speak as Jesus meant them: as a real warning that was really fulfilled, which strengthens faith in his words and removes needless fear.

Many believers have lived in fear that Jesus would say “I never knew you” to them despite their faith. Heard in context, the warning is against empty religious profession that rejects God's ways, aimed first at a generation that rejected him. Those who heeded Jesus escaped. The lasting lesson is the same: knowing God means trusting and following him, and God has not given us a spirit of fear.
2 Timothy 1:7.
1 John 4:18: perfect love casts out fear.
Luke 21:28: straighten up, your redemption is drawing near.
Others warn that removing the fear of final judgement can weaken the call to holiness (2 Corinthians 5:10-11).
What warnings are still about the future?
Those about the resurrection of all the dead and the final judgement: John 5:28-29, Acts 17:31, Romans 2:5-16, 2 Corinthians 5:10, Hebrews 9:27 and Revelation 20:11-15.

These texts speak of all people, all the dead, and the whole world, without first-century time limits. Paul told the Athenians God has fixed a day to judge the world by the man he raised. All must appear before the judgement seat of Christ. These keep the hope and seriousness of the gospel intact.
